title: Who do you say I am? (Matthew 16:13–20)
hook: Peter answers first, and is given a name meaning rock and the keys of the kingdom

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter walks on water: he stepped out, sank as a man of oligopistos, and was caught. Your line was he catches the sinking. What step did you take? Today a new stretch begins: Jerusalem and the last week. Day fifty-seven.

People ask what you do for work, where you're from, what you're into. It's rare that someone asks who you think they are. Matthew sets this scene in the far north, in the region of Caesarea Philippi, a town whose very name honored Caesar. Jesus and his disciples are walking, and he asks them an easy question first: what are people saying about me? Then a hard one. Today's word: the keys.
screen: `WHO DO YOU THINK THEY ARE?` → `CAESAREA PHILIPPI, FAR NORTH.` → `AN EASY QUESTION, THEN A HARD ONE.`

segments.voice: The easy question, in the King James Bible: "Whom do men say that I the Son of man am?" The answers come quickly. Some say John the Baptist, back from the dead. Some say Elijah. Others, Jeremiah, or one of the prophets. Then he turns it: "But whom say ye that I am?" You. Not the crowds. And Peter answers: "Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God." Christ is the Greek for the Hebrew Messiah: the anointed one, the king God promised. Jesus calls him blessed, and says this didn't come from any human being, but from his Father in heaven. Then he gives Simon a new name: "thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it." There's a pun inside. In Greek, Peter is Petros, and rock is petra. And John's Gospel gives Peter's name in Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke, as Cephas, which it says means a stone; Paul calls him Cephas too. Some readers hear one Aramaic word, kepha, under both halves of the line. Then: "And I will give unto thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven." Keys meant authority, the steward of a house who opens and shuts the doors. Here Christians read differently, and deeply. Catholics understand the rock as Peter himself, with his authority passed on to the bishops of Rome; the keys appear on the papal coat of arms. Orthodox Christians honor Peter as first among the apostles, and many of their teachers read the rock as Peter's confession of faith, with authority held by the bishops together. Many Protestants read the rock as that confession, or as Christ himself. The question itself reads the same in every Bible: who do you say I am?
screen: `WHOM DO MEN SAY THAT I AM?` · `BUT WHOM SAY YE?` · `PETROS, PETRA, CEPHAS.` · `THE KEYS: WHO OPENS AND SHUTS.` · then, large: `THOU ART THE CHRIST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit comfortably, and let your breathing slow. Now let the question come to you, just as it came to them. Not what your parents said. Not what your church says, or your friends, or the internet. Who do you say he is? A teacher. A prophet. The Christ. A question mark. Someone you're still meeting. There's no wrong answer in the privacy of your own head, and nobody's grading it. Just be honest with yourself. If you pray, you can bring your answer to God as it is. The bell holds the time.
The keys. The authority to open and shut, given to Peter, the rock, after he answered the hard question. Churches read the keys in different ways.
Your line: the question is for you. Today, when someone asks what you think, pause and give your own answer, not the crowd's. Day fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the Chair of Saint Peter on February 22, and churches East and West keep Saints Peter and Paul on June 29. Many Christians describe coming to faith as answering this question for themselves, and some churches ask it in confirmation or at baptism.

fork.reveal: Peter answers first, and Jesus calls him blessed, gives him a name meaning rock, and promises him the keys.

original.note: Greek: Peter, a stone. Beside petra, a rock, it makes the pun at the heart of this story.

trapdoor: what you thought: the keys are for Saint Peter at the pearly gates.
what it means: Peter answers the hard question and is given a new name and the authority to open and shut, and the question is passed on to every reader.

what a scholar hears: keys echo Isaiah 22:22, where a royal steward is given the key of the house of David, and whether the rock is Peter or his confession is a long-running debate between the churches.

notes: Opens the part 'Jerusalem and the last week' (weeks 9–10, days 57–70).
Caesarea Philippi: near the springs at Banias, a shrine of Pan, and a city named for Caesar Augustus by Philip the tetrarch. Script says 'shrines to other gods'; confirm.

Church readings of 'this rock': Catholic (Peter and his successors, the bishops of Rome); Orthodox (Peter honored as first; many Fathers read the rock as Peter's confession of faith; authority exercised by bishops together); many Protestants (the confession, or Christ). These summaries need a careful Keeper review for fairness to each church.
Crossed keys on the papal coat of arms; confirm.
Keys and Isaiah 22:22 (Eliakim, 'the key of the house of David'); a common scholarly link.
Chair of Saint Peter, February 22 (Catholic); Saints Peter and Paul, June 29 (widely kept).

Fresh review (days 57–74): hook no longer claims Caesarea Philippi was 'full of shrines' (not in the text); the Aramaic pun is now sourced to John 1:42 (Cephas, 'a stone') and the reconstructed Aramaic is given as some readers' view; cut 'Silence, probably', 'first as usual', 'All of them' and 'one of the oldest debates'.
